summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed declaratory and permanent injunctive relief against a juvenile officer who removed all of a school's boarding students using stale and inaccurate ex parte petitions and, as to many children, no court order at all, rejecting his claims of judicial and Eleventh Amendment immunity.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling circuit authority for Nebraska on § 1983 relief against a child welfare official for unlawful removal, including the unavailability of judicial immunity.
key_cases.quote: Waddle removed all boarding students from HCA without notice or opportunity to be heard, using stale or inaccurate information, and without exigent circumstances

key_cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit held that the father's and children's substantive and procedural due process claims failed because the officials' reliance on the abuse allegations did not shock the conscience and a petition, emergency hearing and post-deprivation hearing followed the removal within days.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the federal § 1983 framework — Fourth Amendment seizure plus procedural and substantive due process — under which a wrongful removal claim from Nebraska would be litigated.
key_cases.quote: In child removal cases, the meaningful time and manner requirement means that the state must hold a hearing promptly after removal.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit held that Rooker-Feldman did not bar the student's Fourth Amendment claim but that the social worker's good faith reliance on the ex parte protective custody order was reasonable, so he was entitled to qualified immunity on the seizure claim.
key_cases.relevance: A removal is unlawful under this framework where the ex parte order rests on omissions or stale information so serious that reliance on it was unreasonable.
key_cases.quote: The ex parte order was not so lacking in indicia of probable cause as to render Diercks's reliance on it unreasonable.

key_cases.holding: The court held that an ex parte temporary detention order is not itself a final, appealable order, that henceforth the information supporting such an order must be presented by affidavit of a person with knowledge of the relevant facts, and that the mother's due process rights were satisfied because she received a meaningful opportunity to be heard at the subsequent detention hearing.
key_cases.relevance: A removal carried out without a supporting affidavit and without a prompt, meaningful hearing is the paradigm of the procedural defect this decision identifies.
key_cases.quote: Due process principles therefore require that the mother have been given a meaningful opportunity to be heard on the issue of whether a detention order should have been issued.

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Carmelo G.
key_cases.holding: The court held that a delay of more than eight months between entry of an ex parte temporary custody order and the protective custody order was unreasonable and violated the mother's procedural due process rights.
key_cases.relevance: An extended, unexcused delay in providing the post-removal hearing renders the continued deprivation of custody constitutionally infirm.
key_cases.quote: due process rights include the right to be free from an unreasonable delay in providing a parent a meaningful hearing after the entry of an ex parte temporary custody order
